brief.what: The federal government suspended the provincial government of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and implemented emergency measures, including internet shutdowns and road blocks, to curb protests demanding the release of Imran Khan. While the government claims the action is necessary to protect the population from terrorism, critics view it as a political maneuver to suppress dissent.
brief.who: The main actors include the federal government, which authorized the emergency; the PTI party, led by the imprisoned former Prime Minister Imran Khan; and the Pakistani military, which analysts believe holds the true power behind the decision.
brief.context: Imran Khan has been imprisoned since August 2023 on corruption charges he claims are politically motivated. His party, the PTI, has governed the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province for 13 years, creating a significant power struggle between the provincial opposition and the federal administration.
brief.why: The federal government states the emergency was required to counter terror threats, though they provided no immediate evidence. Analysts suggest the move aims to neutralize the PTI's growing pressure and capitalize on the military's current confidence in its international standing.

items.title: AI is less regulated than milk, says Microsoft president
items.summary: Microsoft President Brad Smith is calling for global safety regulations for artificial intelligence, arguing that current oversight is less stringent than that applied to consumer goods like milk and washing machines. He advocates for mandatory incident reporting and independent government vetting to mitigate risks posed by rogue AI agents.

also.title: Microsoft president says AI faces fewer safety rules than milk in call for global regulation
also.note: Fox Business frames the story by explicitly highlighting the call for 'global regulation' in its headline.

brief.what: Brad Smith, president of Microsoft, stated that AI currently faces fewer safety regulations than common household products. He proposed implementing 'emergency brakes' or kill switches, mandatory incident reporting for AI breaches, and independent government evaluation of new AI technologies.
brief.who: Brad Smith, the president of Microsoft, is the primary advocate for these regulations, while President Donald Trump represents the opposing view that the sector should remain self-regulated to maintain a competitive edge against China.
brief.context: The debate follows growing concerns from industry experts regarding AI's potential threat to humanity, leading to recent discussions between the White House and major tech firms like OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google DeepMind regarding voluntary, morally binding safety commitments.
brief.why: Smith argues that self-regulation is insufficient because it only governs responsible companies, leaving risks from less scrupulous actors unaddressed. He believes the UK is uniquely positioned to lead global standards due to its technical capability and the AI Security Institute.
brief.next: Smith hopes to bring stakeholders together to establish formal, global regulatory frameworks, though he acknowledges the current US administration's preference for a less restrictive, self-regulatory approach.
